datasets.description: CFI is used by government EM as a goal for the coordination of restoration and post disaster economic re‐development and in coordination with infrastructure service providers. This measure is intended to improve communication at county EOCs and other coordination centers during any type of emergency event. This alignment, as well as planning during peace time, ensures that community services are restored in a flexible and coordinated manner.Infrastructure service providers, such as electricity, gas, water, telecom, debris management, etc., use CFI as a guideline in the development and execution of their restoration processes and related priority rankings. It is understood that in the aftermath of an emergency event, it may take days or weeks to restore the critical infrastructure, depending on the severity of the event. The restoration approach is predicated on the type and geographical area of damage.Since “safety of life” is paramount during restoration and recovery, in the immediate aftermath of an event, restoration of the first four types of CFI 1 facilities will be most critical (hospitals, emergency shelters, main fire stations and water/wastewater facilities). These facilities will be given priority in sequence from top to bottom and all facilities are not equally weighted.

datasets.title: Heat Vulnerability Index
datasets.description: This dataset contains the US Census Bureau 2020 Census Block Groups for the State of Florida with selected fields from the 2017-2021 American Community Survey (ACS). Some of the fields included in this dataset are total population, education, and housing and economic characteristics. This data is at the block group level. The ACS was designed to replace the long-form of the decennial census. The ACS is a survey that releases data annually. ACS data are survey estimates distributed for 1-, 3-, and 5-year time periods. The 5-year estimates are the only time period estimates that provide data at the block group level. This data is designed for use within the Florida Department of Transportation Efficient Transportation Decision Making Process (ETDM). However, the subset of ACS fields included herein is useful for a variety of applications and uses.

datasets.title: SewerBasin
datasets.description: Utilities Sewer Basins in Pinellas County, Florida. Sewer Basin Area polygon data was orginally developed to help with tracking “gravity” sewer asset inspections and Smoke testing analysis. A Pinellas County Utilities Sanitary Sewer Basin is a defining area of gravity fed sewage and private property pumping station sewage that utilizes gravity flow into it's particular pressurized Lift/Pump Station that manages the basin's sewage output to our treatment plants. Sewer Basins are named and relate to the Pump Station that handles the basin area's sewage output. Sewer Basins can also include sewage output from several adjacent sewer pump stations, acting as a receiver of sewage for the continued conveyance journey to our treatment plant. Some pump stations are used in pressurized system boosting and may not have a related Sewer Basin. The data contained herein is offered “as is,” with no claim or warranty as to its accuracy or completeness. The data is for reference only and should not be considered to be of survey precision. datasets.description: Residential Capacity Utilization Methodology Maximum Allowed Units are estimated by multiplying a parcel’s gross acreage by the maximum residential density indicated by its Future Land Use (FLU) category (e.g., R-10 = 10 units per acre, R-20 = 20 units per acre, and R-35 = 35 units per acre). Fractional results are rounded down to the nearest whole unit, with a minimum of one unit for parcels with a positive calculated capacity below one unit. Capacity Utilization (%) is calculated by dividing the actual number of residential units by the estimated maximum allowed units and multiplying by 100. Aggregated Bin Utilization (%) is calculated by dividing the sum of actual residential units by the sum of estimated maximum allowed units within each bin and multiplying by 100. These estimates are based on FLU density and parcel acreage. datasets.title: S_FLD_HAZ_AR
datasets.description: The National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) data incorporates all Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) databases published by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), and any Letters of Map Revision (LOMRs) that have been issued against those databases since their publication date. It is updated on a monthly basis. The FIRM Database is the digital, geospatial version of the flood hazard information shown on the published paper FIRMs. The FIRM Database depicts flood risk information and supporting data used to develop the risk data. The primary risk classifications used are the 1-percent-annual-chance flood event, the 0.2-percent-annual-chance flood event, and areas of minimal flood risk. The FIRM Database is derived from Flood Insurance Studies (FISs), previously published FIRMs, flood hazard analyses performed in support of the FISs and FIRMs, and new mapping data, where available. The FISs and FIRMs are published by FEMA. The NFHL is available as State or US Territory data sets. Each State or Territory data set consists of all FIRM Databases and corresponding LOMRs available on the publication date of the data set. The specification for the horizontal control of FIRM Databases is consistent with those required for mapping at a scale of 1:12,000. This file is georeferenced to the Earth's surface using the Geographic Coordinate System (GCS) and North American Datum of 1983.NFHL Layer for Hillsborough County, Florida was downloaded from FEMA Flood Map Service Center (https://msc.fema.gov/portal/home) and reprojected to NAD_1983_StatePlane_Florida_West_FIPS_0902_Feet Coordinate System. curatedUpdates.terms: The ArcGIS item instructs users to check source, scale, accuracy, and currentness; it requests acknowledgement of the Florida Regional Planning Councils and Florida Division of Emergency Management.
